The midterm elections have put Democrats in control
of both the House and the Senate.
How is President Trump responding?
NPR's Maura Liasen takes a look.
He has said he's willing to work with Democrats
to make deals, but if they can't agree,
he'll become Mr. Vito.
But he's also done something that better communicates
how he's planning to go forward.
He promoted Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff.
Miller is the deputy chief of staff now,
and he has promoted the hardest of hard lines
on any number of issues, primarily mass deportations.
He believes in unchecked executive power,
and by choosing Miller, Trump is showing
that he is ready for a lot of confrontation
with an opposition Congress.
More than a dozen races in the House are still to be called,
but the Democrats could have as much
as an 80 seat majority starting in January.
In the Senate, Democrats now have 54 seats,
but they could pick up two more in the races
in Mississippi and Alaska, which are still to be called.
It could take weeks before the results are in in Alaska.
Nearly 60 people have been killed in Yemen
following Saudi airstrikes over the past two days.
NPR's Aya Batrawi says damage is also reported
in Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis say Saudi attacks on a village
in the Governorate of Sana'a killed 33 civilians,
among them 13 children and eight women.
The Houthis said Saudi forces launched attacks
on several homes in the area,
and then targeted roads used by rescue crews.
There were other deadly Saudi airstrikes in Yemen,
including the Houthis say in Hodeidah,
where a man and his five children were killed.
The UN says the resumption of all-out war in Yemen
has displaced 300,000 people since August.
Meanwhile, the Houthis say they targeted
a high-rise tower in the Saudi capital, Riyadh,
belonging to oil company Aramco.
Videos show smoke rising from the center of the tower
as fire sprinklers spray water out from broken windows.
Aya Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
The flood waters have receded across southwest Colorado.
Residents there are just starting to assess the damage
after back-to-back floods swamped the region.
At least 700 homes in Archuleta County have been affected.
Colorado Public Radio's Steena Sieg reports.
Many are around the small town of Pagosa Springs,
where the San Juan River
nearly hit a historic high November 1st,
more than four feet above major flood stage.
Local pastor John Duncan with Centerpoint Church
has been helping residents.
He says they're resilient, but many are overwhelmed.
It's just heartbreaking as you watch the memories
of your children and the treasures
that you've kept floating around in your house,
completely ruined.
Duncan is hosting dozens of out-of-town church members
helping clean up the devastation.
For NPR News, I'm Steena Sieg in Grand Junction, Colorado.
You're listening to NPR.
One cyclist in North Carolina has been killed
and several others injured
after they were hit by a car during a community ride.
Bradley George of member station WUNC has the story.
A group of about 20 cyclists
from the Capital City Cycle Club
were on a Saturday morning ride on a two-lane road
near the town of Holly Springs, south of Raleigh.
The State Highway Patrol says the driver,
76-year-old Donald Robert Morris Jones,
was intoxicated and tried to flee the scene
but drove into a ditch after hitting the cyclists.
Holly Springs Fire Chief Leroy Smith.
Just be aware of people that are out riding bikes.
They have rights to be on the road, too,
so kind of yield to them and be cautious
when you're riding around bicycles.
Morris Jones has been charged with multiple felony counts
and will make his first court appearance on Monday.
For NPR News, I'm Bradley George in Chapel Hill.
Google, Meta, and TikTok have filed separate lawsuits
seeking to block a California state law
designed to protect children from the risks of social media.
The social media companies argue
the law violates their First Amendment rights.
The law is scheduled to go into effect on January 1st.
It prohibits tech companies from offering addictive feeds,
endless scrolling, and auto-played videos
to children under 16.
Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill into law
in September.
California's Attorney General
says the office remains committed
to defending state laws that protect children online.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.
